sections.authorBiography: Herman Melville was born in New York City on 1 August 1819. After his merchant father's bankruptcy and death he went to sea, sailing on a whaler in 1841 and jumping ship in the Marquesas; his South Seas adventures Typee (1846) and Omoo (1847) were popular. Moby-Dick (1851) and the works that followed sold poorly, and from 1866 he worked for nineteen years as a customs inspector in New York. He died on 28 September 1891, largely forgotten; his reputation was revived in the 1920s.
sections.historicalContext: Wall Street in the 1840s–50s was becoming the centre of American finance. Before photocopiers and typewriters, legal documents were copied by hand by scriveners (copyists) paid by the page. Melville wrote the story after the commercial failure of Moby-Dick (1851) and Pierre (1852), when he himself was being asked to write what the market wanted.

publicationAndReception.publication: First published anonymously in two parts in Putnam's Monthly Magazine, November and December 1853, as "Bartleby, the Scrivener. A Story of Wall-Street"; collected in The Piazza Tales (1856).
publicationAndReception.then: Modestly noticed; Melville's reputation was in decline and he died in 1891 largely forgotten.
publicationAndReception.now: Since the Melville revival of the 1920s it has been one of the most discussed American stories; "I would prefer not to" has become a catchphrase for passive resistance, cited in discussions of the Occupy Wall Street movement (2011).

sections.overview: An elderly Wall Street lawyer narrates his encounter with Bartleby, a quiet copyist he hires, who one day begins answering every request with "I would prefer not to."
sections.whyItMatters: The story speaks to modern experiences of meaningless work, burnout and the limits of compassion.

spoilerOverview.text: Bartleby stops working entirely and refuses to leave; the lawyer moves his office rather than evict him. Bartleby is taken to the Tombs prison, where he refuses to eat and dies. The lawyer then hears a rumour that Bartleby once worked in the Dead Letter Office.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Bartleby, the Scrivener.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Bartleby, the Scrivener: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

wholeBookTest.title: Bartleby, the Scrivener: whole-book test

items.prompt: What does the narrator finally do?
Where had Bartleby worked before, according to rumor?

In the line “Owing to the great height of the surrounding buildings, and my chambers being on the second floor, the interval between this wall and mine not a little resembled a huge square cistern.”, what does “cistern” most nearly mean?

In the line “At any rate, upon the occasion in question, I strove to drown my exasperated feelings towards the scrivener by benevolently construing his conduct.”, what does “benevolently” most nearly mean?
As used in the story (“Owing to the great height of the surrounding buildings, and my chambers being on the second floor, the interval between this wall and mine n”), what does “cistern” mean?
options: a prayer asking God's help as part of a religious service

items.prompt: As used in the story (“At any rate, upon the occasion in question, I strove to drown my exasperated feelings towards the scrivener by benevolently construing his c”), what does “benevolently” mean?
As used in the story (“These sad fancyings—chimeras, doubtless, of a sick and silly brain—led on to other and more special thoughts, concerning the eccentricities ”), what does “chimeras” mean?
options: the ritual placing of a corpse in a grave
not having enough money to pay for necessities

items.prompt: As used in the story (“I believe that this wise and blessed frame of mind would have continued with me, had it not been for the unsolicited and uncharitable remark”), what does “obtruded” mean?
options: a prayer asking God's help as part of a religious service

items.prompt: As used in the story (“Like a very ghost, agreeably to the laws of magical invocation, at the”), what does “invocation” mean?
options: a prayer asking God's help as part of a religious service

answerKey.answer: a prayer asking God's help as part of a religious service

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Bartleby, the Scrivener teaches about passive resistance. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Herman Melville develops passive resistance in Bartleby, the Scrivener. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Herman Melville develops passive resistance across Bartleby, the Scrivener. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of Bartleby, the Scrivener (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of passive resistance. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of passive resistance in Bartleby, the Scrivener. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Herman Melville's choices in Bartleby, the Scrivener (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of passive resistance, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places Bartleby, the Scrivener's treatment of passive resistance in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on passive resistance in Bartleby, the Scrivener that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on passive resistance in Bartleby, the Scrivener. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about passive resistance in Bartleby, the Scrivener, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on passive resistance in Bartleby, the Scrivener, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
